explanation: Fires on many kinds of token in question or problem-statement text and in lists, e.g. 'or' between listed items ('drugs, devices or diagnostics'), 'little is known', 'deal with', 'want to know more', 'how could I'. No clear single trigger; the common thread may be a predictable continuation in informal or expository prose.

Fires on the second word of hedging or concessive discourse phrases: 'at [least]', 'not [even]', 'don't [even]', parenthetical '[however]', 'or [rather]', 'after [all]', 'suffice', 'be that [as]'. Strongest on 'least' after 'or at' and 'even' after a negation. Weak on other function words.

Fires inside CJK text (Chinese/Japanese characters, especially in code strings, comments or names) and on boilerplate in software license headers ('AUTHORS OR COPYRIGHT HOLDERS', 'Apple Inc. and the'), plus scattered code tokens. The two main sources are CJK characters and license/code boilerplate.

Fires on website boilerplate and legal or license boilerplate: cookie notices ('more personalised [service]', 'best [experience]'), 'visit [again]', 'click', 'if [not], write to the' in GPL headers, 'distributed [on/in]'. Strongest in cookie-consent sentences. Ordinary prose does not activate it.

Fires on a pronoun or possessive (his, her, their, my, your, he, they) when it follows a copula or a relative-clause head and refers back to a person in a role or relationship ('Tommy is [her] coach', 'King was [his] mother's name', 'someone [he] considers', 'the company [they] work for'). Weaker on pronouns in other positions.

Fires on a mixture: dotted Java/C# member names in code ('e[[.printStackTrace]]', '.StoredProcedure', '.AlertDialog'), the second token of well-known proper names ('King Abdullah', 'New Yorker', 'Charles E. Schumer'), and literary words such as 'silently', 'wrath', 'stifling'. The thread may be a highly predictable token completion, but the examples share no clear concept.

Fires on a very wide range of tokens: random characters in tokens and hashes, relational prepositions ('member [of]', 'in line [with]', 'partnered [with]', 'directly [between]'), code punctuation and name fragments. No unifying pattern is visible.

Fires on the main verb (or verb-like word) of a clause right after its subject or modal, in narrative or explanatory prose: 'you'll be [able]', 'if they [find]', 'Things [got]', 'there [exists]', 'I [get]', 'you [can]', 'the problem [went] away'. Weaker on other words.

Fires on a subword token holding a vowel plus 'd' (ad, ud, od, ed, id, Had, Gad, Rad, Ped, Hod, Nad) inside a rare proper name or technical word split into pieces (Guadagnini, Prudential, Hodges, Hadley, cadaver, radial). Strong when the fragment is word-initial or mid-word in a name.

Fires on assorted function words and nouns in conversational or forum prose ('lots [of]', 'grateful for [the]', 'wrong [questions]', 'talk [about]', 'Chances are [you]', 'this [question]'). No clear selectivity for the token or its context.

Fires on fixed boilerplate phrases in software license headers ('you may not [use] this file', 'with or [without] modification', 'NOT LIMITED [TO]', 'except [in] compliance') and on forum or blog formulas ('Thanks in [advance]', 'honored [if] you read'). Strongest on 'use' in the Apache license line.
Fires strongly on 'year' in 'last year', and on a mixed set of other tokens: 'today's', 'as [was]', 'good', 'Wherever', code identifiers. The 'last year' part is clear. The rest looks unrelated.
Fires on a broad mix: word pieces in medical terms (debridement, cruciate, melanoma), product or listing text, code identifiers, plural endings and general nouns. No consistent trigger.

Fires on a mixture of tokens: subword pieces of rare names and technical terms ('Gh'outa, 'bul'losa, 'bench'marks, 'ign'iter, Dill'ash'aw), code identifiers, and a few ordinary nouns or commas. It may track the middle of multi-token rare words, but many examples fall outside that.

Fires on word-initial or mid-word subword pieces of formal or legal Latinate words ('Conf'essional/Confederate/conflicts, 'Acc'ompaniment, CRIM'INAL', 'AP'PELLATE) and of non-English words ('Fi'anna, Czech or Polish diacritic pieces). It also fires on some verbs in narratives ('conducting', 'took', 'received').

Fires on a mix of function words and punctuation that come early in a sentence or short title: '(' after a name, 'was' after a person's name in court opinions, commas, Portuguese or Russian word pieces, numbers in identifiers. No single concept.

Fires mainly on the occupation or role noun in a sports biography ('is a Spanish football[er]', 'soccer [player]', 'Sports[people]', 'red[shirt]'), and on other words in athlete or person profiles. It also fires on a few unrelated tokens ('blood group [is]', 'Person'nel).

Fires on a mixture: 'Redistributions' and 'and [the] ... authors' in license headers, 'Continue [reading]', the head noun of named organisations or awards ('Peace [Corps]', 'Tony [Award]'), and some code tokens. No single thread.

Fires on nouns naming a commercial service or the provider of one in business or advertising text ('SEO [company]', 'start-up strategy and [services]', 'Benjamin Franklin [Plumbing]', '[professionals]', 'repairs', 'installation'). It also fires moderately on law-firm names in legal citations.
Fires on many unrelated tokens: commas in number tuples, '(' opening a parenthetical, 'the' after a preposition, 'site' in 'web site', 'benefit' in patent boilerplate. No discernible pattern.

Fires on tokens in Stack-Overflow-style technical questions that describe a problem ('am [not] sure', 'and [not] just', 'use [it]', 'same [request]', 'whereas', 'but'), and on parts of code or data examples. The common thread is loosely the help-seeking question genre rather than any specific token.
